title: Single-ventricle palliation: Norwood, bidirectional Glenn and Fontan completion
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Congenital Heart Disease: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 42 (Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome and Fontan Operation)
AHA Scientific Statement on Single Ventricle and Fontan Circulation

steps.say: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is the prototype single-ventricle malformation. Severe hypoplasia of the left ventricle, mitral valve, and aortic arch renders the left heart incapable of supporting systemic circulation. The right ventricle must support both pulmonary and systemic vascular beds in parallel.
steps.tx: **Hypoplastic left heart syndrome** features severe underdevelopment of the left-sided cardiac structures, including aortic and mitral atresia. The morphological **single right ventricle** functions as the sole systemic pumping chamber, supporting both systemic and pulmonary vascular beds through an obligatory parallel circulation.

left.title: Normal Biventricular Circulation
points: Left ventricle generates high systemic pressure
Right ventricle pumps low-pressure deoxygenated blood

right.title: HLHS Single Ventricle Circulation
points: Obligatory parallel circulation fed by solitary right ventricle
Systemic cardiac output depends entirely on ductus arteriosus
Pulmonary and systemic flows compete dynamically

steps.say: The Norwood stage one operation establishes unobstructed systemic output and controlled pulmonary blood flow in the neonatal period. The surgeon constructs a neoaorta by amalgamating the main pulmonary artery with the hypoplastic aortic arch. Atrial septectomy ensures unrestricted pulmonary venous return.
steps.tx: The neonatal **Norwood procedure** achieves three vital surgical goals: constructing a wide **neoaorta** by anastomosing the pulmonary trunk to the hypoplastic aortic arch, performing an **atrial septectomy** to prevent pulmonary venous hypertension, and providing calibrated systemic-to-pulmonary **pulmonary blood flow**. Performing this complex neonatal reconstruction establishes reliable systemic tissue perfusion while safeguarding the pulmonary vascular bed.

nodes.label: Transect main pulmonary artery from branching pulmonary arteries
Amalgamate pulmonary trunk with hypoplastic aorta using homograft patch
Resect interatrial septum to create unrestrictive mixing

steps.say: Surgeons balance the pulmonary circulation using either a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt or a Sano right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery conduit. The Blalock-Taussig shunt connects the innominate artery to the pulmonary artery, whereas the Sano conduit originates directly from the right ventricular free wall.
steps.tx: Pulmonary blood flow is established using either a **modified Blalock-Taussig shunt** from the innominate artery or a **Sano shunt** connecting the right ventricle directly to the pulmonary artery. The Sano conduit eliminates diastolic runoff, preserving **coronary perfusion pressure** and preventing sudden cardiac arrest.

left.title: Modified Blalock-Taussig Shunt (mBTS)
points: 3.5 mm PTFE tube from innominate to pulmonary artery
Continuous systemic runoff lowers diastolic blood pressure
Vulnerable to coronary steal and ventricular ischemia

right.title: Sano RV-PA Conduit
points: 5 mm PTFE conduit from RV infundibulum to PA bifurcation
Flow occurs purely in systole without diastolic runoff
Preserves diastolic coronary driving pressure in neonates

steps.say: The bidirectional Glenn procedure unloads the single ventricle by removing upper body volume work. The superior vena cava is anastomosed to the right pulmonary artery. This creates passive pulmonary flow from cerebral venous return directly into the pulmonary vascular bed without ventricular work.
steps.tx: The bidirectional Glenn procedure provides vital **ventricular unloading** by eliminating volume work from the single ventricle. Direct cavopulmonary connection establishes **passive pulmonary flow**, channeling upper body **cerebral venous return** directly into the pulmonary arterial tree without passing through a subpulmonary pump.

nodes.label: Confirm low pulmonary vascular resistance (< 2 to 3 Wood units)
Transect superior vena cava from the right atrium
End-to-side anastomosis of SVC to right pulmonary artery
Take down previous neonatal systemic-to-pulmonary shunt

steps.say: The Fontan completion serves as the final stage of palliation, performed at two to four years of age. An extracardiac conduit carries and directs inferior vena caval blood directly into the pulmonary arteries. Passive venous return now bypasses the heart completely, separating pulmonary and systemic circulations.
steps.tx: The final stage is the **extracardiac conduit Fontan**, performed at 2 to 4 years of age. A polytetrafluoroethylene tube graft connects the inferior vena cava directly to the pulmonary artery, establishing **passive pulmonary perfusion** and directing all desaturated blood through the lungs without a subpulmonary pump.

rows: Relieves systemic arch obstruction; calibrated parallel shunt
SVC to PA shunt; unloads single ventricle volume overload
IVC to PA conduit; completes total cavopulmonary separation

steps.say: Successful Fontan physiology requires strict baseline hemodynamic criteria. The mean pulmonary artery pressure must remain below fifteen millimeters of mercury, with pulmonary vascular resistance under two to three Wood units. Low pulmonary impedance is essential because blood flows through the lungs without a ventricle.
steps.tx: Successful Fontan function requires strict **hemodynamic Fontan criteria**: mean pulmonary artery pressure under 15 mmHg, **pulmonary vascular resistance < 2 to 3 Wood units**, and preserved single ventricular systolic function. Without a subpulmonary ventricle, passive pulmonary transit relies entirely on low **downstream resistance**.

rows: Permits passive transpulmonary gradient driving flow
Avoids cavopulmonary stasis and low cardiac output
Guarantees low filling pressure in systemic ventricle

steps.say: Creating a small surgical fenestration in the conduit improves early postoperative stability. A four to five millimeter communication between the Fontan conduit and the common atrium allows right-to-left shunting. This pop-off decompression maintains cardiac output during periods of transient pulmonary vasoconstriction.
steps.tx: Surgeons frequently construct a 4 to 5 mm **Fontan fenestration** connecting the extracardiac conduit to the atrium. This intentional right-to-left pop-off decompression augments systemic **cardiac output maintenance** at the expense of mild cyanosis, significantly curbing prolonged postoperative **pleural effusions** and ascites.

left.title: Fenestrated Fontan
points: Permits right-to-left decompression during pulmonary strain
Reduces early chest tube drainage and hospital stay

right.title: Non-Fenestrated Fontan
points: Complete physical separation without intracardiac shunt
Higher incidence of prolonged ascites and pleural drainage

steps.say: The abnormal Fontan circulation produces significant late systemic complications across decades. Elevated central venous pressure and low cardiac output lead to protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, and progressive hepatic fibrosis. Regular multidisciplinary surveillance is required to manage failing Fontan physiology.
steps.tx: Chronic venous hypertension and diminished cardiac output trigger late **failing Fontan physiology**. Long-term systemic attrition manifests as **protein-losing enteropathy**, life-threatening **plastic bronchitis**, cardiac cirrhosis, and ventricular arrhythmias, often necessitating late heart transplantation evaluation in specialized adult congenital clinics. Lifelong dedicated clinical follow-up is mandatory to detect and manage these insidious systemic and circulatory Fontan sequelae.

rows: Mesenteric venous congestion causing enteric lymph loss
Profound hypoalbuminemia, ascites, elevated fecal a1-antitrypsin
High lymphatic pressures leak mucin casts into airways
Expectoration of branched bronchial casts, asphyxiation
Chronic hepatic venous congestion and sinusoidal fibrosis
Bridging fibrosis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma risk
